hero.title: School Support
hero.subtitle: How Elmbrook School District turns a student robotics team into a district-wide access program — covering costs, opening spaces, and removing the institutional barriers that keep most teams from scaling.

impact.label: District Partnership
impact.text: GEarheads operates inside a three-way institutional partnership with the Elmbrook School District superintendent, Brookfield Central principal, and the school's athletic director. This structure means every major decision — from budget line items to facility scheduling — has an administrative champion at each level. It is rare for a single FTC team to have formal buy-in from all three tiers of school administration, and it is the reason the team can offer access to programs that most peer teams fund entirely out-of-pocket.

facets.question: How does the district partnership actually work?
facets.description: The GEarheads' relationship with Elmbrook School District is not a sponsorship in the traditional sense — no check is written directly to the team. Instead, it is a layered institutional endorsement that unlocks every other benefit. The superintendent has formally recognized the team as a model for STEM access within the district, meaning that when the team requests resources or scheduling accommodations, the request carries administrative weight rather than competing with standard club requests. The Brookfield Central principal manages day-to-day access: practice room scheduling, storage space, after-hours building access, and the ability to host visiting FLL and FTC teams on school grounds. The athletic director's involvement is the most structurally unusual piece — by treating FTC as an extracurricular athletics program rather than a generic club, the team gains access to athletic department infrastructure and formal school event support. Together, these three relationships mean the team does not operate as a volunteer club that rents space from a school; it operates as an embedded program with institutional standing. This matters enormously for scaling: when you want to host a 26-team tournament, you need a building administrator who can authorize it overnight, not a six-week approval queue.

facets.question: What do FLL and FTC registration and field costs actually cover — and why does the district paying them matter?
facets.description: Competing in FIRST programs is not free, and the costs are high enough to function as a barrier of entry for many families. A single FTC season requires team registration fees, game field element kits (which run several hundred dollars and change every year with the new game), and tournament entry fees. FLL registration and field set costs are structurally similar. Left to individual families or fundraising, these costs create a pay-to-play dynamic that makes robotics a sport for households that can absorb several hundred dollars annually per student. Elmbrook School District covers these line items — registration and field hardware — for both FLL and FTC programs affiliated with Brookfield Central. The practical effect is that no student at BCHS who wants to participate in FIRST robotics is turned away because their family cannot afford the entry costs. This is not a partial subsidy; it is full cost coverage for the core program participation fees. The significance compounds over multiple seasons: a student who joins FLL in fifth grade and advances to FTC by ninth grade has had four-to-five seasons of registration and equipment costs absorbed by the district. The team's ability to pipeline students from FLL into FTC — and to recruit broadly rather than only from families who can self-fund — depends entirely on this cost-coverage structure.

facets.question: How has school support increased physical robotics space over time?
facets.description: Physical space is consistently one of the hardest constraints for high school robotics teams. Most clubs share a room with three other activities, have no dedicated storage, and cannot leave a half-assembled robot out overnight. The GEarheads' administrative relationships have progressively improved this situation at Brookfield Central. Early seasons involved shared classroom space during off-hours. As the team's relationship with administration deepened, dedicated storage for the robot, field elements, and tools was allocated. More significantly, the team has been able to use the school's larger open spaces — gymnasium floor space, hallways, and the school's fabrication resources — for practice runs, field setup, and hosting visiting teams. Increased school robotics spaces means both dedicated team workspace and access to facilities at scale for outreach events. When the team hosted the Rookie Qualifier for 26 FTC teams, the event required gymnasium floor space, judging rooms, a pit area, and parking coordination — none of which is possible without administration committing building resources. The trajectory has been consistent: each season, the school's investment in allocated space has grown, which in turn expands what the team can build, practice, and host.

facets.question: What is the ~$100 BCHS club fee model, and how does it fit into the broader cost picture?
facets.description: Brookfield Central High School charges a standardized club fee — currently approximately $100 annually — that applies to student participants in the GEarheads program. This fee structure is the district's formal mechanism for cost-sharing: it is low enough to be accessible to the vast majority of BCHS families, and it is offset by the district's coverage of registration and field hardware, meaning the fee goes toward team operations rather than program entry. In practical terms, the $100 fee per student covers shared costs like tools, consumable materials (hardware, wiring, 3D-print filament), and team supplies that are not subsidized at the district level. It is also the formal mechanism through which students enroll in the BCHS robotics program rather than operating as an informal after-school group — the fee creates an official student-activity relationship that unlocks school liability coverage, equipment borrowing policies, and teacher-supervisor assignment. Compared to the total cost of fielding a competitive FTC team — which can run several thousand dollars per season when you include registration, field elements, parts, travel, and equipment — the $100 student contribution is a deliberately small ask. The gap is bridged by district subsidies, corporate sponsorships from partners like GE HealthCare and Milliman, and the team's own fundraising. The club-fee model is also equitable by design: students who cannot pay the fee are handled through a school-administered hardship waiver process, ensuring the nominal amount does not itself become a barrier.
